cues.text: Called to Be Holy
Every Christian is called to be a saint.
That claim can sound bold, even presumptuous, until we remember what the word actually means.
A saint is someone who now shares fully in the life of God — someone whose answer to grace was carried, by God’s mercy, all the way home.
The Church does not reserve holiness for a spiritual elite.
She proclaims it as the ordinary vocation of every baptized person, however extraordinary the individual stories may look from the outside.
We often picture saints as remote figures in stained glass, untouched by struggle.
Read their actual lives, and a different picture emerges: men and women who doubted, failed, and began again, letting grace do in them what they could not do alone.
Two Meanings of One Word
The word saint carries two related meanings.
In the broad sense, Scripture uses it for every believer in a state of grace — St.
Paul greets whole congregations as “the saints,” meaning simply the holy people of God, still on the road.
In the narrower, more familiar sense, a capital-S Saint is someone the Church has formally recognized as already sharing the joy of heaven, whose life she holds up as a sure model.
Both senses point to the same reality.
Canonized saints are not a different species of Christian.
They are the ones whose answer to grace has already reached its completion — proof, for the rest of us still walking, that the path really leads where it promises.
How the Church Recognizes a Saint
Canonization is not a prize the Church awards.
It is the Church declaring, after long and careful examination, that a particular life is a trustworthy sign of holiness — safe to imitate, safe to ask for prayers.
The process usually opens locally, years after death, when a bishop names the person a Servant of God.
Investigators comb the writings and testimony gathered about the life for evidence of heroic virtue — faith, hope, and love lived to an extraordinary degree, in ordinary circumstances.
If Rome concurs, the title Venerable follows.
Beatification, which allows the title Blessed, normally requires a miracle attributed to the person’s intercession after death, examined by physicians and theologians alike.
A martyr may be beatified without one, since laying down one’s life for Christ is already the clearest possible witness.
A second such miracle, after beatification, is normally required for canonization — the Church’s declaration that this person is now with God and worthy of veneration everywhere.
Many of the Church’s earliest saints — the apostles, the martyrs, the first virgins and monks — predate this whole process.
Their holiness was recognized by the faithful and confirmed by bishops and popes over centuries, long before Rome centralized the procedure in the later Middle Ages.
Ask Them to Pray for Us
Catholics do not worship saints.
Worship — what the Church calls latria — belongs to God alone; giving it to any creature would be idolatry.
What we offer the saints is veneration: honor, gratitude, and above all, a request.
We ask them to pray for us, exactly as we might ask a friend still living, except that these friends already stand in the fullness of God’s presence.
This confidence rests on the Communion of Saints — the Church in heaven, the Church being purified, and the Church still on pilgrimage on earth, bound together as one body in Christ (CCC 946).
Those who dwell with God, the Catechism teaches, do not cease to intercede for us still on the road (CCC 956).
Feast Days and Patrons
Every saint on this timeline carries a feast day — the anniversary the Church keeps, usually the day of death, understood as a birth into eternal life.
Many also carry a patronage: a particular concern, place, or trade the faithful have long entrusted to their intercession, often rooted in some detail of the saint’s own life.
Neither is arbitrary.
Both are the Church’s way of keeping the saints close — not distant statues, but companions for a particular day, a particular trade, a particular trouble.
A Life Fully Given
The saints do not ask to be admired from a distance.
They ask to be imitated — not by repeating the outward details of their lives, but by making the same total gift of self to the same God who made them holy.
Whoever they were, wherever they lived, they show us still that an ordinary human life, given without reserve, is exactly the raw material of sainthood.
